title: Hong Shao Rou (Red-Braised Pork Belly)
subtitle: Slow-braised pork belly in a rich soy and caramel sauce
excerpt: Hong shao rou is one of the great Chinese comfort dishes. Pork belly is braised low and slow in soy sauce, sugar, and spices until the fat becomes silky and the sauce turns into a deep, glossy glaze. This is patient cooking that rewards every minute it is given.
sourceNotes: Hong shao rou (red-braised pork belly) is one of the most beloved dishes in Chinese home cooking. The technique of slow-braising pork belly in soy sauce, sugar, and rice wine until the fat turns glossy and tender is found across China. Mao Zedong was said to have eaten it daily; it remains a national comfort food.

content.text: Hong shao rou is a long-cook dish. The blanching step at the start is worth doing -- it keeps the braise clean and removes any impurities from the pork. After that, time does the work. The caramel step is important for colour and flavour: take it to a deep amber before the pork goes in.

items.prepNote: use 700g pork belly if available -- cut into 4cm chunks
use Shaoxing rice wine or dry sherry

content.text: Blanch the pork belly in boiling water for 5 minutes. Drain and rinse. This removes impurities and helps the final braise stay clean.

In a wide, heavy pan, heat 1 tablespoon of oil and add the brown sugar. Stir over medium heat until the sugar melts and turns a deep amber caramel -- about 3 minutes. Watch carefully so it does not burn.
Add the pork pieces. Turn quickly to coat in the caramel.
Add the soy sauce, honey, Shaoxing wine, ginger, garlic, star anise, cinnamon, and stock. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat to a low simmer. Cover and braise for 60 to 75 minutes, turning the pork every 20 minutes, until the fat is meltingly tender.
Remove the lid and increase heat. Reduce the sauce for 10 minutes until thick and glossy. Serve with steamed rice and greens.

items.symptom: Sauce is too thin at the end
items.cause: Did not reduce with the lid off
items.fix: After the pork is tender, remove the lid and turn the heat to medium-high. Stir frequently and let the sauce bubble down until it coats the pork thickly -- this takes 10 to 15 minutes.

content.text: Hong shao rou is Chinese comfort food at its best. The pork belly becomes silk-soft after long braising. The red-brown sauce is sweet, salty, and deeply savoury. The dish is popular in Shanghai, Hunan, and Hangzhou, each with slight regional variations. It is eaten with plain white rice.
